procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated the 18th September 1953 of the Travancore-Cochin High Court at Ernakulam in 0. P. No. 41 of 1952.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner filed a writ petition in the Travancore High Court against Respondent No. 1 and Respondent No. 2 (Indian Income-Tax Investigation Commission) for a writ of prohibition prohibiting the Respondents from holding an enquiry into the cases registered as Evasion Cases Nos. 1 & 2 of 1125 or from holding an investigation into the income of the petitioner from the year 1940 to the last completed assessment year. The Travancore High Court held that the Respondent No. 2 had all the powers that the Travancore Commission had under Travancore Act XIV of 1124 and no more and granted the writ prohibiting respondents from conducting an enquiry into years other than 1942 and 1943.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Both the parties appealed to the Supreme Court against the order of the High Court. A preliminary objection to the jurisdiction of the High Court to entertain the writ petition was repeated in the Supreme Court by the Attorney-General. The appeals were brought to the Supreme Court under Article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution of India.

decision.conviction_status: Altered from section 302 of the Indian Penal Code to 304 of the Indian Penal Code
decision.sentence_status: Modified to five years' rigorous imprisonment

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioner's argument that a voluntary submission conferred jurisdiction on the High Court to issue a writ against respondent 2 could be considered on appeal, given that no writ was in fact issued against that respondent and the petitioner had not appealed that part of the High Court's decision.

facts: The petitioner argued that respondent 2 had voluntarily submitted to the jurisdiction of the High Court by stating in an affidavit that they were prepared to follow the court's directions.
The High Court did not, in fact, issue a writ against respondent 2; it only issued a writ against respondent 1.
The petitioner did not file an appeal against the High Court's decision to not issue a writ against respondent 2.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the petitioner was asking it to rule on whether the High Court had jurisdiction over respondent 2 based on a voluntary submission.
However, the Court found it unnecessary to decide this point for two key reasons.
First, the High Court never actually exercised jurisdiction by issuing a writ against respondent 2.
Second, since the petitioner had not appealed the High Court's failure to issue a writ against respondent 2, that specific issue was not properly before the Supreme Court for review.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument and declined to express any opinion on the matter. It reasoned that since no writ was actually issued against respondent 2 by the High Court, and the petitioner had not appealed that part of the decision, the question of whether a voluntary submission had conferred jurisdiction was moot and not a subject for the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the petitioner's argument that a voluntary submission conferred jurisdiction on the High Court to issue a writ against respondent 2 could be considered on appeal, given that no writ was in fact issued against that respondent and the petitioner had not appealed that part of the High Court's decision.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner argued that both respondents had voluntarily submitted to the jurisdiction of the High Court. This was evidenced by an affidavit where they stated they were 'fully prepared to shape their proceedings in accordance with the directions of the Court'. This submission, it was contended, invested the High Court with the jurisdiction to issue a writ against respondent 2.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (represented by the Attorney-General) argued that the High Court of Travancore-Cochin had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition against respondent 2.

statutes.act_name: Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947 (Act XXX of 1947)

cases.case_name: Suraj Mall Motha & Co. v. A. V. Visvanatha Sastri and another
cases.principle: The procedure for investigation prescribed by Act XXX of 1947 was of a summary and drastic nature, constituting a departure from the ordinary law of procedure, and was detrimental and discriminatory to persons subjected to it compared to the procedure under the Indian Income-tax Act.

After the introduction of section 34(1-A) into the Indian Income-tax Act, the classification in section 5(1) of Act XXX of 1947 was no longer a valid defense against a charge of discrimination under Article 14, as the new provision in the Income-tax Act covered the same class of persons but provided a less prejudicial procedure.

cases.case_name: Budhan Chowdhury and others v. The State of Bihar
cases.principle: To pass the test of permissible classification under Article 14, two conditions must be fulfilled: (i) the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons grouped together from others left out, and (ii) that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute. Article 14 condemns discrimination by both substantive and procedural law.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A statute that vests discretion in an administrative body to selectively apply the law is not unconstitutional for violating the equal protection clause, provided the statute itself lays down a clear and definite legislative policy or objective. The discretion conferred is not unguided; it must be exercised in conformity with that policy, and any classification made by the administrative body is valid if it has a rational relation to the objective of the legislation. However, if the administrative body classifies persons or things on a basis that has no rational relation to the legislative objective, its action can be annulled.
obiter: The court did not express an opinion on whether a party's voluntary submission to the jurisdiction of a High Court would be sufficient to invest that court with the jurisdiction to issue a writ against that party.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court declined to express any opinion on whether the respondents had voluntarily submitted to the High Court's jurisdiction because the issue was not properly before it on appeal. The High Court had not, in fact, issued a writ against respondent 2, and more importantly, the petitioner had not appealed that specific part of the High Court's decision, thereby waiving the right to argue the point.
legal_tests_applied: Appellate Procedure: An appellate court will not consider an argument related to a part of a lower court's decision that was not appealed by the aggrieved party.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioner failed to appeal the part of the High Court's decision where no writ was issued against respondent 2, which procedurally barred the Supreme Court from considering the argument.
The question of jurisdiction over respondent 2 was rendered moot for the purpose of the appeal because the High Court did not actually issue a writ against that respondent.
why_respondent_won: The respondent prevailed on this point by default because the Court refused to entertain the petitioner's argument on procedural grounds, without needing to address the merits of the jurisdiction question.
